title: AI is a bubble, just like dot-com
content_html:
August 5, 2026

I tested out having Claude generate the final draft. Results were quite clear that people would not read it lol.

Andrej Karpathy has written large language models the way most of us have written CRUD apps. He was a founding member of OpenAI, ran AI at Tesla, and joined Anthropic this spring to train Claude. He wrote nanoGPT and llm.c, the small readable codebases people use to learn how a language model works end to end.

When Anthropic put Claude inside Slack, he called it “a new paradigm” — the third major redesign of how humans use these systems. Not a website you visit anymore, not an app you install, but “a self-contained, persistent, asynchronous entity with org-wide tools and context, working alongside teams of humans.”

He closed with: “it works and it is awesome.”

The replies had a different read. One of them, in full:

> This is a new paradigm

brother it's a slack integration

I miss the old andrej

— @MatthewFoxAF June 24, 2026

Hold that exchange still for a second. Nobody in it is stupid. That’s what makes it worth understanding.

The same split runs through everything right now, and nothing around it holds still.

Leadership says “use more AI,” and never defines responsible use. Engineers hear it through an older instinct: don’t ship what you don’t understand. Nobody explains how both survive.

Layoff announcements credit AI in the same breath as the earnings beat. A colder fear sits underneath: people who own the AI on one side, people whose work it does on the other, no visible way across.

The ground keeps moving. Prompt engineering was a job title. OpenClaw picked up a hundred thousand GitHub stars and caused a Mac Mini shortage in the same week. Ralph was the future for about a weekend. Context engineering, then harness engineering, then graph engineering. Each was the obvious way to work, right up until the next one was. The gaps keep getting shorter.

And everywhere, teams ship code faster than they can understand it. Ask whoever’s on call.

I’d love to stand cleanly on one side of all this. I can’t. I haven’t written a line of code in about a year. Claude writes it all. These posts too. I read all the code before it ships, and I still feel the difference. Understanding used to be a byproduct of writing the code myself. Now understanding is a separate job.

Both perspectives, one person.

There’s a default way to resolve contradictions like these: decide who’s deluded. “I miss the old andrej” does it in five words: if Karpathy calls a Slack bot a paradigm, something must have happened to Karpathy. Sorting people into right and wrong passes for rigor. It assumes that when two perspectives contradict, one of them must be false.

Our industry tested that assumption once before, at scale.

In March 2000 the NASDAQ peaked above 5,000. By October 2002 it had lost 78 percent of its value. Pets.com IPO’d in February and was gone by November. The sock puppet outlived the company. Betting against it was exactly right.

Amazon lost more than 90 percent of its stock price in the same crash and kept shipping. Within a decade the internet had rearranged retail, news, music, and how you found a job. Betting on Amazon was exactly right too.

Same year. Same technology. “Wildly overhyped” and “changes everything” were both correct at the extreme.

Nobody had to be deluded.

And there were four ways to stand, not two. Short everything: it’s all a bubble. Long everything: it’s all the future. Long Pets.com, short Amazon: backwards twice. Long Amazon, short Pets.com: right twice. The first two are moods about a technology. The last two are judgments about cases. The only thing separating right twice from backwards twice was understanding.

None of it was magic. The information separating a Pets.com from an Amazon was public the whole time. The hard part was knowing what question to ask of it. What could the internet do that nothing before it could? A bookstore with every book in print, yes. Free shipping on forty-pound bags of dog food, no. Most people, watching the same screens, never asked. They picked a mood and waited for the grade.

We’re inside the next one now. That may be the only point the amazed and the unimpressed already agree on: whatever this is, it’s big.

Transformational technology comes along maybe twice in a working life. I was in school for the last one, watching different screens: South Park, Perfect Dark, Conker’s Bad Fur Day. This time I want to understand it while it’s moving: test hypotheses against what happens, and decide how I work while the decision still matters.

You’re inside it too. Your feed has already assigned you a position: be amazed, or be afraid. Both are moods. Understanding isn’t assigned. You have to go get it.

So start where understanding starts. What is the disagreement about?

Mostly not models. There are arguments over which model is best, and over whether open weights beat closed ones. They stay small and almost polite. The real fights are somewhere else. Do you read every line the model writes? Can you ship code you don’t understand? Do passing tests mean it works? Does an AI review count as a review? Every team I know is re-deciding these rules on the fly. Some decide with conviction. More sound like: we don’t know what to do, but we’d better do something.

Model quality enters at one point only: “the models will get so good that none of this will matter.”

Maybe.

So here’s my first hypothesis, stated so you can hold me to it. Models will not become dependable enough, soon enough, to settle these questions for us. If you’re sure that’s wrong, sure that near-flawless output arrives in a year or two, you can stop reading. The questions will answer themselves, and this series with them. I don’t think that’s where we are.

Now set the pieces next to each other. Intelligent people look at one technology and see wildly different things. History says conclusions that far apart can both be correct. And the rule debates run on, team after team, without resolving. Arguments that run this long between capable people are built on assumptions nobody has checked. We’ve already seen one: somebody has to be wrong. The rule debates lean on another that nobody has said out loud. Behind that one is the question that sorted Amazon from Pets.com, aimed at our own work this time.

What did this enable that we couldn’t do before?

Each of those rule debates assumes an answer to it. That’s the question this series works out. One small, checkable step at a time. I’m writing to answer it for myself. You’re welcome to come along and check the work. By the end you won’t need my conclusions. You’ll have your own read on any AI claim that crosses your feed.

Including this one: AI is a bubble, just like dot-com.

Thanks to Emma Bukacek and Tim Pote, who read early drafts and told me what wasn’t working.

sentences.zh: 互联网能做些什么之前它做不到的事情呢？

sentences.en: A bookstore with every book in print, yes.
sentences.zh: 一家书店，每本书都有印刷版，是的。

sentences.en: Free shipping on forty-pound bags of dog food, no.
sentences.zh: 四十磅一袋的狗粮免运费，不。

sentences.en: Most people, watching the same screens, never asked.
sentences.zh: 大多数人看着同样的屏幕，从来没有问过。

sentences.en: They picked a mood and waited for the grade.
sentences.zh: 他们选择了心情并等待成绩。

blocks.html_en: We’re inside the next one now. That may be the only point the amazed and the unimpressed already agree on: whatever this is, it’s big.

sentences.en: We’re inside the next one now.
sentences.zh: 我们现在在下一个里面。

sentences.en: That may be the only point the amazed and the unimpressed already agree on: whatever this is, it’s big.
sentences.zh: 这可能是惊讶者和不为所动的人已经达成的唯一一点：无论这是什么，它都很大。

blocks.html_en: Transformational technology comes along maybe twice in a working life. I was in school for the last one, watching different screens: South Park, Perfect Dark, Conker’s Bad Fur Day. This time I want to understand it while it’s moving: test hypotheses against what happens, and decide how I work while the decision still matters.

sentences.en: Transformational technology comes along maybe twice in a working life.
sentences.zh: 变革性技术在工作生涯中可能会出现两次。

sentences.en: I was in school for the last one, watching different screens: South Park, Perfect Dark, Conker’s Bad Fur Day.
sentences.zh: 我在学校看最后一部，观看不同的屏幕：《南方公园》、《完美黑暗》、《康克的坏毛皮日》。

sentences.en: This time I want to understand it while it’s moving: test hypotheses against what happens, and decide how I work while the decision still matters.
sentences.zh: 这次我想在它移动的同时理解它：根据发生的情况测试假设，并在决定仍然重要时决定我如何工作。

blocks.html_en: You’re inside it too. Your feed has already assigned you a position: be amazed, or be afraid. Both are moods. Understanding isn’t assigned. You have to go get it.

sentences.en: You’re inside it too.
sentences.zh: 你也在其中。

sentences.en: Your feed has already assigned you a position: be amazed, or be afraid.
sentences.zh: 您的提要已经为您分配了一个位置：感到惊讶，还是感到害怕。

sentences.en: Both are moods.
sentences.zh: 两者都是心情。

sentences.en: Understanding isn’t assigned.
sentences.zh: 理解不是分配的。

sentences.en: You have to go get it.
sentences.zh: 你必须去拿它。

blocks.html_en: So start where understanding starts. What is the disagreement about?

sentences.en: So start where understanding starts.
sentences.zh: 因此，从理解开始的地方开始。

sentences.en: What is the disagreement about?
sentences.zh: 有何分歧？

blocks.html_en: Mostly not models. There are arguments over which model is best, and over whether open weights beat closed ones. They stay small and almost polite. The real fights are somewhere else. Do you read every line the model writes? Can you ship code you don’t understand? Do passing tests mean it works? Does an AI review count as a review? Every team I know is re-deciding these rules on the fly. Some decide with conviction. More sound like: we don’t know what to do, but we’d better do something.

sentences.en: Mostly not models.
sentences.zh: 大多不是模型。

sentences.en: There are arguments over which model is best, and over whether open weights beat closed ones.
sentences.zh: 关于哪种模型最好，以及开放权重是否优于封闭权重，存在争议。

sentences.en: They stay small and almost polite.
sentences.zh: 他们身材矮小，而且几乎很有礼貌。

sentences.en: The real fights are somewhere else.
sentences.zh: 真正的战斗在其他地方。

sentences.en: Do you read every line the model writes?
sentences.zh: 你读过模型写的每一行吗？

sentences.en: Can you ship code you don’t understand?
sentences.zh: 你能发送你不理解的代码吗？

sentences.en: Do passing tests mean it works?
sentences.zh: 通过测试就意味着它有效吗？

sentences.en: Does an AI review count as a review?
sentences.zh: AI评论算不算评论？

sentences.en: Every team I know is re-deciding these rules on the fly.
sentences.zh: 我认识的每个团队都在即时重新决定这些规则。

sentences.en: Some decide with conviction.
sentences.zh: 有些人坚定地做出了决定。

sentences.en: More sound like: we don’t know what to do, but we’d better do something.
sentences.zh: 听起来更像是：我们不知道该怎么做，但我们最好做点什么。

blocks.html_en: Model quality enters at one point only: “the models will get so good that none of this will matter.”

sentences.en: Model quality enters at one point only: “the models will get so good that none of this will matter.”
sentences.zh: 模型质量只在某一点上起作用：“模型会变得非常好，以至于这一切都不再重要。”

blocks.html_en: Maybe.

So here’s my first hypothesis, stated so you can hold me to it. Models will not become dependable enough, soon enough, to settle these questions for us. If you’re sure that’s wrong, sure that near-flawless output arrives in a year or two, you can stop reading. The questions will answer themselves, and this series with them. I don’t think that’s where we are.

sentences.en: So here’s my first hypothesis, stated so you can hold me to it.
sentences.zh: 这是我的第一个假设，这样你就可以坚持我的观点。

sentences.en: Models will not become dependable enough, soon enough, to settle these questions for us.
sentences.zh: 模型不会变得足够可靠、足够快地为我们解决这些问题。

sentences.en: If you’re sure that’s wrong, sure that near-flawless output arrives in a year or two, you can stop reading.
sentences.zh: 如果您确定这是错误的，并且确定一两年内会出现近乎完美的输出，那么您可以停止阅读。

sentences.en: The questions will answer themselves, and this series with them.
sentences.zh: 这些问题将会自行解答，本系列也将解答这些问题。

sentences.en: I don’t think that’s where we are.
sentences.zh: 我不认为这就是我们现在的处境。

blocks.html_en: Now set the pieces next to each other. Intelligent people look at one technology and see wildly different things. History says conclusions that far apart can both be correct. And the rule debates run on, team after team, without resolving. Arguments that run this long between capable people are built on assumptions nobody has checked. We’ve already seen one: somebody has to be wrong. The rule debates lean on another that nobody has said out loud. Behind that one is the question that sorted Amazon from Pets.com, aimed at our own work this time.

sentences.en: Now set the pieces next to each other.
sentences.zh: 现在将各个部分并排放置。

sentences.en: Intelligent people look at one technology and see wildly different things.
sentences.zh: 聪明人在看待一项技术时会看到截然不同的事物。

sentences.en: History says conclusions that far apart can both be correct.
sentences.zh: 历史表明，相距甚远的结论也可能都是正确的。

sentences.en: And the rule debates run on, team after team, without resolving.
sentences.zh: 规则的争论一个接一个地持续进行，却没有解决办法。

sentences.en: Arguments that run this long between capable people are built on assumptions nobody has checked.
sentences.zh: 有能力的人之间持续这么久的争论是建立在没有人验证过的假设之上的。

sentences.en: We’ve already seen one: somebody has to be wrong.
sentences.zh: 我们已经看到了这一点：一定有人是错的。

sentences.en: The rule debates lean on another that nobody has said out loud.
sentences.zh: 规则辩论依赖于另一个没有人大声说出的规则。

sentences.en: Behind that one is the question that sorted Amazon from Pets.com, aimed at our own work this time.
sentences.zh: 这个问题的背后是亚马逊从 Pets.com 中分类出来的问题，这次是针对我们自己的工作。

blocks.html_en: What did this enable that we couldn’t do before?

sentences.en: What did this enable that we couldn’t do before?
sentences.zh: 这使我们能够做什么以前无法做到的事情？

blocks.html_en: Each of those rule debates assumes an answer to it. That’s the question this series works out. One small, checkable step at a time. I’m writing to answer it for myself. You’re welcome to come along and check the work. By the end you won’t need my conclusions. You’ll have your own read on any AI claim that crosses your feed.

sentences.en: Each of those rule debates assumes an answer to it.
sentences.zh: 每一个规则辩论都假设有一个答案。

sentences.en: That’s the question this series works out.
sentences.zh: 这就是本系列要解决的问题。

sentences.en: One small, checkable step at a time.
sentences.zh: 一次一小步，可检查。

sentences.en: I’m writing to answer it for myself.
sentences.zh: 我写这篇文章是为了自己回答这个问题。

sentences.en: You’re welcome to come along and check the work.
sentences.zh: 欢迎您过来检查工作。

sentences.en: By the end you won’t need my conclusions.
sentences.zh: 到最后你就不需要我的结论了。

sentences.en: You’ll have your own read on any AI claim that crosses your feed.
sentences.zh: 您将对任何出现在您的推送中的人工智能声明有自己的解读。

blocks.html_en: Including this one: AI is a bubble, just like dot-com.

sentences.en: Including this one: AI is a bubble, just like dot-com.
sentences.zh: 包括这一点：人工智能是一个泡沫，就像互联网一样。

blocks.html_en: Thanks to Emma Bukacek and Tim Pote, who read early drafts and told me what wasn’t working.

sentences.en: Thanks to Emma Bukacek and Tim Pote, who read early drafts and told me what wasn’t working.
sentences.zh: 感谢艾玛·布卡切克 (Emma Bukacek) 和蒂姆·波特 (Tim Pote)，他们阅读了早期草稿并告诉我哪些地方不起作用。

content_html_zh:
2026 年 8 月 5 日

我测试了让克劳德生成最终草案。 结果很明显，人们不会读它，哈哈。

Andrej Karpathy 编写大型语言模型的方式与我们大多数人编写 CRUD 应用程序的方式相同。 他是 OpenAI 的创始成员，在 Tesla 负责人工智能，并于今年春天加入 Anthropic 来培训 Claude。 他编写了 nanoGPT 和 llm.c，这是人们用来学习语言模型如何端到端工作的小型可读代码库。

当 Anthropic 将 Claude 放入 Slack 中时，他称之为“一个新范式”——对人类如何使用这些系统的第三次重大重新设计。 它不再是您访问的网站，也不是您安装的应用程序，而是“一个独立的、持久的、异步的实体，具有组织范围的工具和上下文，与人类团队一起工作。”

他最后说道：“它有效，而且非常棒。”

回复有不同的解读。 其中之一，完整：

> 这是一个新的范式兄弟，这是一个松弛的集成我想念旧的 andrej — @MatthewFoxAF 2026 年 6 月 24 日

让这种交换保持一秒钟。 里面没有人是傻子。 这就是它值得理解的原因。

现在同样的分裂贯穿一切，周围没有任何东西是静止的。

领导层说“更多使用人工智能”，但从未定义负责任的使用。 工程师们通过一种古老的本能听到了这句话：不要发布你不理解的东西。 没有人解释两者如何生存。

裁员公告与业绩好转一样，都归功于人工智能。 一种更冷的恐惧隐藏在下面：一方面是拥有人工智能的人，另一方面是为人工智能工作的人，没有明显的跨越途径。

地面不断移动。 即时工程是一个职位名称。 OpenClaw 在 GitHub 上获得了十万颗星，并在同一周内引发了 Mac Mini 的短缺。 拉尔夫是大约一个周末的未来。 上下文工程，然后利用工程，然后图形工程。 每一种都是显而易见的工作方式，直到下一种为止。 差距不断缩小。

在任何地方，团队交付代码的速度都快于他们理解的速度。 询问值班人员。

我很愿意干净地站在这一切的一边。 我不能。 我大约有一年没有写过一行代码了。 克劳德写下了这一切。 这些帖子也是。 我在发布之前阅读了所有代码，但仍然感受到了差异。 理解曾经是我自己编写代码的副产品。 现在理解是一项单独的工作。

两个视角，一个人。

解决此类矛盾有一个默认的方法：决定谁被欺骗了。 “我想念老安德烈”用五个字表达了这一点：如果 Karpathy 将 Slack 机器人称为范例，那么 Karpathy 一定发生了什么事。 将人们严格地分为正确和错误的通行证。 它假设当两种观点相互矛盾时，其中一种必定是错误的。

我们的行业之前曾大规模测试过这一假设。

2000 年 3 月，纳斯达克指数达到 5,000 点以上的峰值。 到 2002 年 10 月，它的价值已经缩水了 78%。 Pets.com 于 2 月份进行了 IPO，并于 11 月份退出。 袜子木偶的寿命比公司还要长。 押注它是完全正确的。

亚马逊在同一次崩盘中股价下跌了 90% 以上，但仍继续发货。 十年之内，互联网重新安排了零售、新闻、音乐以及找工作的方式。 押注亚马逊也是完全正确的。

同年。 相同的技术。 “过度炒作”和“改变一切”都是极端正确的。

没有人必须被欺骗。

有四种站立方式，而不是两种。 做空一切：一切都是泡沫。 渴望一切：这就是未来。 做多 Pets.com，做空 Amazon：倒退两次。 做多 Amazon，做空 Pets.com：两次正确。 前两个是对技术的情绪。 最后两项是对案件的判决。 唯一区分正确两次和倒退两次的就是理解。

这一切都不是魔法。 Pets.com 与亚马逊的分离信息一直都是公开的。 困难的部分是知道要问什么问题。 互联网能做些什么之前它做不到的事情呢？ 一家书店，每本书都有印刷版，是的。 四十磅一袋的狗粮免运费，不。 大多数人看着同样的屏幕，从来没有问过。 他们选择了心情并等待成绩。

我们现在在下一个里面。 这可能是惊讶者和不为所动的人已经达成的唯一一点：无论这是什么，它都很大。

变革性技术在工作生涯中可能会出现两次。 我在学校看最后一部，观看不同的屏幕：《南方公园》、《完美黑暗》、《康克的坏毛皮日》。 这次我想在它移动的同时理解它：根据发生的情况测试假设，并在决定仍然重要时决定我如何工作。

你也在其中。 您的提要已经为您分配了一个位置：感到惊讶，还是感到害怕。 两者都是心情。 理解不是分配的。 你必须去拿它。

因此，从理解开始的地方开始。 有何分歧？

大多不是模型。 关于哪种模型最好，以及开放权重是否优于封闭权重，存在争议。 他们身材矮小，而且几乎很有礼貌。 真正的战斗在其他地方。 你读过模型写的每一行吗？ 你能发送你不理解的代码吗？ 通过测试就意味着它有效吗？ AI评论算不算评论？ 我认识的每个团队都在即时重新决定这些规则。 有些人坚定地做出了决定。 听起来更像是：我们不知道该怎么做，但我们最好做点什么。

模型质量只在某一点上起作用：“模型会变得非常好，以至于这一切都不再重要。”

Maybe.

这是我的第一个假设，这样你就可以坚持我的观点。 模型不会变得足够可靠、足够快地为我们解决这些问题。 如果您确定这是错误的，并且确定一两年内会出现近乎完美的输出，那么您可以停止阅读。 这些问题将会自行解答，本系列也将解答这些问题。 我不认为这就是我们现在的处境。

现在将各个部分并排放置。 聪明人在看待一项技术时会看到截然不同的事物。 历史表明，相距甚远的结论也可能都是正确的。 规则的争论一个接一个地持续进行，却没有解决办法。 有能力的人之间持续这么久的争论是建立在没有人验证过的假设之上的。 我们已经看到了这一点：一定有人是错的。 规则辩论依赖于另一个没有人大声说出的规则。 这个问题的背后是亚马逊从 Pets.com 中分类出来的问题，这次是针对我们自己的工作。

这使我们能够做什么以前无法做到的事情？

每一个规则辩论都假设有一个答案。 这就是本系列要解决的问题。 一次一小步，可检查。 我写这篇文章是为了自己回答这个问题。 欢迎您过来检查工作。 到最后你就不需要我的结论了。 您将对任何出现在您的推送中的人工智能声明有自己的解读。

包括这一点：人工智能是一个泡沫，就像互联网一样。

感谢艾玛·布卡切克 (Emma Bukacek) 和蒂姆·波特 (Tim Pote)，他们阅读了早期草稿并告诉我哪些地方不起作用。
